title: Loch Ness Monster Sightings Jump From 6 to 15 This Year, and a Researcher Explains What Witnesses May Really See
byline: Sydney Anderson Published: Nov 19 2026, 4:16 AM EST
excerpt: Reported Loch Ness Monster sightings rose from 6 to 15 in 2026. A researcher explains what witnesses likely saw and what DNA testing found.
content:
Reported sightings of the Loch Ness Monster have more than doubled this year, climbing to 15 in 2026 from six in 2025, according to the Official Loch Ness Monster Sightings Register. But a scientist who has spent years studying those reports says the jump does not point to anything new in the Scottish loch.

Charles Paxton, a research fellow in statistical ecology at the University of St Andrews, told Fox News Digital he saw nothing special about the increase. "The numbers fluctuate a lot year on year," he said.

The bigger story is what the sightings reveal about human perception. Paxton doubts an unknown creature lives in Loch Ness, but he does not think witnesses are lying. Instead, he says people are seeing real things on the water and interpreting them through expectation and culture.

Waves, Wakes and Wildlife on the Water

Paxton has suggested that Nessie has many sources rather than one. Animals in the loch, boat wakes, wind-driven waves and floating vegetation can all create shapes that look like a moving body or a series of humps.

Loch Ness is well suited to fooling the eye — it is a long, narrow, very deep lake, and boat wakes can travel and persist across its surface long after the boat has passed. Wide stretches of open water offer few reference points, which makes it hard to judge an object's size or distance. A swimming deer, a diving bird, a floating log or a group of otters can easily look larger and stranger than it is.

Paxton's earlier research found that many reported sightings happened closer to shore than people might assume, not just as distant specks. His team has also used costumes and props in experiments to study how people describe unexpected encounters, including a test with a person in a gorilla suit to mimic Bigfoot reports.

Sightings Rise and Fall With Culture

Paxton has spent years building a statistical catalog of more than 1,000 recorded sightings since 1933, looking for patterns that natural explanations could account for. Witnesses have ranged from local residents and hotel owners to visiting celebrities and clergy, which helps explain why researchers take the reports seriously as data even while doubting a monster.

The modern Nessie phenomenon began in 1933 and 1934, when a run of reports drew crowds of tourists. A new road along the loch's shore opened up views of the water at about the same time. Interest faded, then revived in the 1960s when the Loch Ness Investigation Bureau began collecting sightings. Since the 1970s, reports have generally declined, with year-to-year swings.

Culture shapes what people expect to see. A St Andrews study led by Paxton found that the discovery of long-necked marine reptile fossils in the 19th century appears to have influenced how people describe lake monsters. Paxton is now researching how cultural influences may contribute to reported sightings.

Sightings can also cluster around busy tourist seasons, organized searches and media attention, since more eyes on the water means more unusual things get reported. Three of this year's reported sightings came in March, July and August.

Clues From the 2018 DNA Survey

In June 2018, a team led by geneticist Neil Gemmell of New Zealand's University of Otago collected about 250 water samples from across Loch Ness and analyzed the environmental DNA, or eDNA, that living things shed into the water. According to Live Science, the survey detected traces of more than 3,000 species living in or beside the loch.

It found no reptile DNA of any kind, ruling out the popular plesiosaur theory as far as the samples could show. The team also found no evidence of sturgeon, catfish or sharks. What it did find was a very significant amount of eel DNA at nearly every sampling location.

Gemmell said a giant eel was at least a plausible explanation for some sightings, but the data could not show whether the DNA came from one huge eel or many ordinary ones. The common European eel is not known to grow anywhere near monster size. "People love a mystery," Gemmell said when presenting the results, according to RNZ.

The eDNA survey has limits too — it sampled the loch at one time of year, and DNA breaks down in water over days to weeks. Still, it remains the most comprehensive biological census of Loch Ness ever conducted.

Judging a Sighting Yourself

For visitors to the Scottish Highlands, a little observation science can make a Nessie hunt more fun and more informative. If you see something unusual, note the time, the wind direction, and whether any boats passed recently. Try to film with a fixed landmark, such as the shoreline or Urquhart Castle, in the frame to help judge size and distance.

Patience helps too. Most odd shapes resolve into something ordinary within a minute or two of careful watching.

Be skeptical of viral clips and photos. Lake monster images are easy to misread or edit, and the most famous historic Nessie photo, taken in 1934, was later revealed to be a hoax. Footage that lacks a clear scale or location should be treated as unverified.

Nature World News previously covered a large volunteer search of the loch in 2023. Searches like that are likely to continue, and so are sightings. The science suggests the most reliable answer is that people are seeing eels, birds, deer, waves and wakes, and that Nessie lives on as a mystery of human perception.

What Readers Want to Know

How many Loch Ness Monster sightings were reported in 2026? Fifteen, up from six in 2025, according to the Official Loch Ness Monster Sightings Register.

Does the increase mean something new is in the loch? No. Researcher Charles Paxton says the numbers fluctuate a lot from year to year.

What do witnesses most likely see? Animals such as eels, birds and deer, along with boat wakes, wind waves and floating vegetation.

What did the 2018 DNA survey find? More than 3,000 species, no reptile DNA, and a large amount of eel DNA throughout the loch.

Could Nessie be a giant eel? It is considered plausible for some sightings, but the DNA could not distinguish one giant eel from many normal-sized ones.

How can I evaluate a sighting? Note wind and boat traffic, film with a landmark in view for scale, and be cautious about viral images.
